title: I'm a game sound designer building a sound generator that only does UI sounds for now. It's free, and I'd love feedback
author: WrittenWaveform
selftext:
Hey all,

I've been doing game audio for a while (sound design and implementation in Wwise/FMOD/UE5). For the past few months I've been building something on the side: an AI sound effect generator made specifically for games.

Being upfront about where it is:

It's still a work in progress. Right now the model only does UI sounds: clicks, hovers, confirms, backs, menu open/close, errors, that kind of thing.

It's trained to make sounds that work as game UI, not generic "AI audio" that you then have to cut up and fix.

More categories will come once UI is solid. I'd rather have one thing working well than ten things half-working.

It's free to use while it's in development.

What I'm after is honest feedback from people actually making games:

Do the sounds work in your project as-is?

What breaks, sounds off, or annoys you?

What would you want it to make next?

Link: [www.resoundle.com](https://app.resoundle.com/login.html)

Happy to answer anything about how it works or the audio side of things. Roast it if needed, that's the point of putting it out early.

replies.author: WrittenWaveform
replies.body:
Fair question! Yes, it asks you to sign up right now. Generating audio costs money on my end, so the login stops it getting hammered by bots. It's still completely free, no card or anything, and takes about 10 seconds with Google but is capped at 50 generations per user.

If the login put you off, I would like to know. Was it the sign up itself, or was it unclear that it's free? Trying to make that first step as smooth as possible.

replies.author: WrittenWaveform
replies.body: Fair to be cautious with any random login on the internet! It's just me, a game sound designer, plus a small team. The login is a standard Google sign in and only gives us your name and email. No passwords stored on our end, no access to anything else.

replies.author: WrittenWaveform
replies.body: >Heard, and clearly the top request here. Going to let people try a few generations without signing up, and only ask for an account if you want to keep generating or save sounds. Will update this thread when it's live.

comments.author: Fun-Term616
comments.body:
It works but I won't use the sounds. My issue with making game sounds through AI is yes I can ask it to make a sound and if the sound is real like a sword slash it will make the sound of an actual sword but the sounds I want aren't realistic but tone driven. 

I'll give an example. I played Majora's Mask as a kid and the start of a new day the screen has a pop up and makes some strange double thud sound. I still remember that sound and it stresses me out because the whole tone of that game was "You're running out of time" I have no idea what the sound was but it matched the pressure and anxiety that is the games tone. 

There is like this hidden knowledge on sounds and the emotions they convey. I can recognize certain sounds and the feelings they give but I can't explain. If I could put a prompt in that said "I need a menu click sound that fills me with the dread of being hunted" and the sound that came out was something you'd hear playing slender man. It needs the theory behind sounds.

replies.author: WrittenWaveform
replies.body:
This is honestly a very useful feedback I've gotten, thank you for writing it out.

You are describing exactly what I care about as a sound designer. Most AI audio tools are trained to make things sound real, but game UI is almost never about realism. It's about what the sound makes you feel and what it tells you about the game's world. That Majora's Mask sound is a great example. It doesn't need to sound like anything real, it just has to make you feel uneasy. A lot of that comes from things like low, dull weight instead of a bright "ding," a rhythm that feels like a heartbeat or a clock, and no pleasant resolution at the end. Sound designers do this stuff by instinct, and you are right that it's hard to put into words.

That's the gap I want this tool to close. Being able to type "menu click that fills me with dread" and get something that actually feels like that is the goal, not "realistic button click."

comments.author: Toastti
comments.body: You need to understand registration for an account is a massive roadblock. You have to show multiple samples of the sounds you generate on the homepage without having to login if you ever want to get people interested in this

replies.author: WrittenWaveform
replies.body: You're right, and you're not the only one who's said it. That's three people in this thread now, so message received. Asking for a sign up before anyone has heard a single sound is backwards. I'm considering adding a sample section to the homepage so you can hear what it makes before committing to anything. Appreciate you being blunt about it. Out of curiosity, what kind of sounds would you want to hear in those samples to judge whether it's worth trying? Clicks and confirms, or more stylized stuff like sci-fi or fantasy UI?

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body: Why would I register? If it s free why do you need my data?

replies.author: WrittenWaveform
replies.body:
>Totally fair question, and I'd rather be upfront about it.  
>  
>Two reasons. First, every generation costs us real GPU money, so the login stops bots from draining the free tier. Second, yes, we do look at usage data: what people are trying to generate, which sounds get downloaded vs. regenerated, and roughly where users are from. That's how I figure out what to build next and where the model is falling short. If 40% of people are typing "sci-fi menu click" and getting meh results, that tells me exactly what to fix.  
>  
>We don't sell any of it or share it with anyone. It's purely to make the tool better. If that's still not your thing, completely understand. Curious though, would you be more comfortable if you could try a few generations without an account first?

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body: Fair. But I don't sign up for a service I can't even try first. And I would love to try

replies.author: WrittenWaveform
replies.body: Noted! will figure out a way for you to try it without logging in

replies.author: WrittenWaveform
replies.body: Working on letting you hear and try sounds without an account.

comments.author: Creative_Ad_2049
comments.body: Thanks for sharing this is super nice. Do you plan on scaling it by introducing more categories?

replies.author: WrittenWaveform
replies.body: Thank you, really appreciate it! And yes, that's the plan. I started with UI because it's the most consistent category to get right, and I wanted it to sound properly game-ready before branching out. More categories are coming once each one is solid enough that I would actually use it in a project myself.
